title: Unitree Robotics Soars 629% in Shanghai Debut as China's Physical-AI Cluster Goes Public
subhead: Unitree's Star Market listing opened at a US$66 billion valuation, capping a week in which China's humanoid-robot sector — led by AgiBot — consolidated its global lead even as Washington moved to ban Chinese robots. The IPO is a bellwether for how Beijing's physical-AI push is being priced by capital markets.

sections.heading: Unitree's Blockbuster Debut Puts a Price on China's Physical-AI Bet
sections.body: Hangzhou-based Unitree Robotics surged 629 per cent above its IPO price on its Shanghai Star Market debut Wednesday, opening at 1,100 yuan per share and valuing the humanoid-robot maker at roughly 445 billion yuan (US$66 billion), according to SCMP. The company had priced its offering at 150.8 yuan a share, expecting to raise about 6.1 billion yuan (US$904 million) in a listing widely seen as a bellwether for mainland China's emerging humanoid sector. The debut coincided with the opening of the World Robot Conference in Beijing, giving the sector a high-profile stage.
sections.whyItMatters: The valuation — roughly seven times the IPO price — shows how aggressively Chinese capital is pricing the physical-AI thesis, and gives Beijing's robotics champions a deep pool of domestic funding to scale against US and Japanese rivals.

sections.heading: AgiBot Overtakes Unitree as World's Top Humanoid Vendor
sections.body: Even as Unitree grabbed the headlines, research firm Smart Analytics Global (SAG) reported that Shanghai-based AgiBot had overtaken Unitree as the world's largest humanoid-robot vendor in the first half of 2026, capturing 44 per cent of the global market after shipping roughly 8,400 units from January to June — a 562 per cent year-on-year surge, SCMP reported. AgiBot's diversified portfolio (bipedal A-series, compact X-series, wheeled G-series) outpaced Unitree's concentration on its flagship G1 model, which shipped about 5,900 units for a 31 per cent share. Both companies are racing toward public listings amid the physical-AI boom.
sections.whyItMatters: The leadership shift shows China's robotics sector is not a single-company story but a fast-moving cluster where multiple players can scale quickly — complicating any single-point response by competitors or regulators.

sections.heading: Taiwan Think Tank Warns of a 'China Shock' in Physical AI
sections.body: Taiwan's DSET think tank warned that Beijing's whole-of-nation push into physical AI could produce another 'China shock' for global industry, according to Nikkei Asia. The warning frames China's robotics drive — spanning humanoids, industrial automation and embodied AI — as a coordinated industrial-policy effort rather than isolated company successes, echoing the pattern of earlier Chinese dominance in solar, batteries and EVs.
sections.whyItMatters: The framing shifts the robotics race from a company-level competition to a state-vs-state industrial contest, which is likely to invite more export controls and allied industrial-policy responses.

sections.heading: Washington Bans New Chinese Robots and Power Inverters
sections.body: The Trump administration on Tuesday banned imports of new Chinese robots and power inverters, the latest in a series of tech crackdowns, SCMP reported. The move targets the same humanoid and industrial robotics sector now surging in Chinese capital markets, and extends US restrictions on Chinese hardware into a new category beyond semiconductors and telecoms gear.
sections.whyItMatters: The ban signals that robotics — not just chips — is now a front in the US-China technology rivalry, even as Chinese vendors dominate global humanoid shipments.

sections.heading: SK Hynix Unveils $28.6bn Buyback as Memory Boom Mints Cash
sections.body: South Korea's SK Hynix announced a 40 trillion won (US$28.6 billion) share buyback plan Wednesday, part of a shareholder-return program that raises its target to over 50 per cent of free cash flow, Nikkei Asia reported. The move underscores the memory chip maker's confidence after record second-quarter earnings, even as it continues expanding production capacity. The buyback comes amid a broader AI-driven memory boom that has reshaped the sector's finances.
sections.whyItMatters: Record memory profits are now being recycled into shareholder returns and capacity expansion simultaneously — a sign the AI memory cycle is generating enough cash to both reward investors and fund the next build-out.

sections.heading: Xiaomi Profit Slumps 43% on Memory Crunch and EV Competition
sections.body: Chinese smartphone maker Xiaomi saw net quarterly income nearly halve, down 43 per cent, on a memory-cost crunch, weak demand and intensifying EV competition, Nikkei Asia reported. The profit squeeze illustrates how the AI memory boom is a two-sided story: chipmakers like SK Hynix are minting record profits while downstream hardware makers absorb higher component costs.
sections.whyItMatters: The divergence between memory producers and device makers shows the AI boom is redistributing value up the supply chain, squeezing consumer-hardware margins even as chip suppliers thrive.

sections.heading: Nokia to Wind Down Mainland China Operations
sections.body: Finnish telecoms equipment maker Nokia plans to close almost all of its mainland China sites by year-end, cutting most of its China workforce after more than 40 years in the market, SCMP reported. The retreat marks a further consolidation of China's telecoms-equipment market around domestic vendors and a continued pullback of Western network suppliers from the country.
sections.whyItMatters: Nokia's exit underscores how network sovereignty and market access dynamics are pushing Western telecoms vendors out of China, deepening the split between Chinese and Western telecom supply chains.

bottomLine: China's physical-AI sector moved decisively into the capital markets this week, with Unitree's 629 per cent debut valuing the humanoid-robot cluster at tens of billions of dollars even as AgiBot claimed the global sales lead and Washington moved to ban Chinese robots. The robotics race is now being priced by markets and contested by states in parallel. Meanwhile, the AI memory boom continued to mint cash for chipmakers like SK Hynix while squeezing downstream hardware makers like Xiaomi, and Nokia's retreat from mainland China underscored the deepening decoupling of telecom supply chains. The through-line: AI's economic and geopolitical dividends are concentrating in upstream suppliers and in China's state-backed hardware champions.
